rows.name: Casting Test
textFields:
You can cast Spells you have memorised or those you can read from a grimoire (see page 237). To cast a Spell, make a Challenging (+0 SL) Language (Magick) Test.

If the Casting Test is successful, calculate the SL and compare it to the CN of the Spell. If the SL is equal to or greater than the CN, you cast the Spell as explained in the Spell description. If not, the Spell fails.

rows.name: Critical Casting
textFields:
If you roll doubles on a successful Casting Test, you cause a Critical Casting. Roll on the Minor Miscast Table (page 238). Note that the Instinctive Diction Talent may help mitigate the risk of Miscasts. If you Critically Cast, you may choose one of the three extra effects:

•  Critical Damage: If the Spell causes Damage, it also inflicts a Critical Wound to the Hit Location struck (or the Body if none is defined).

•  Total Power: The Spell is cast. You may add the tens digit of your Casting Test to your SL for the purpose of Overcasting.

•  Unstoppable Force: The Spell may not be dispelled (see page 237).

Petty Spells do not cause Critical Casting or a Minor Miscast on a Critical.

rows.name: Duration
textFields: A successfully cast Spell lasts for its Duration. If you wish for a Spell to last for a shorter time than it normally would, you must declare how long the Spell will remain in effect when the Spell is cast. Once the Spell is in effect, it can only be ended before the duration elapses by dispelling it.

rows.name: Fumbled Casting
textFields: If you roll doubles on a failed Casting Test, you Fumble the cast. Roll on the Minor Miscast Table.

rows.name: Ingredients
textFields:
You may channel your magic through an appropriate ingredient before unleashing your Spell. This protects against Miscasts as the attuned ingredient absorbs the worst of any magical backlash.

To use an ingredient while casting, declare that you are doing so before making the Casting Test. Ingredients reduce Miscast level by one step: reducing a Major Miscast to a Minor one, or reducing a Minor Miscast to no effect.

The ingredient is consumed by the process, even if no Miscast was rolled. Ingredients must be bought for a single Spell and normally cost half the Spell’s CN in silver shillings.

rows.name: Magic Missiles
textFields: Magic missiles are damage-causing Spells. When a magic missile is successfully cast, reverse the dice on the Casting Test to determine where the target is struck using the Hit Locations table (page 164). To calculate Damage, add your Willpower Bonus to the Spell’s listed Damage. This Damage is reduced by the target’s Toughness Bonus and Armour Points as usual.

rows.name: Spellcasting Limitations
textFields:
You must speak or sing to cast Spells. If your voice is inhibited, the GM should increase the Difficulty of Casting Tests by one step.

When Spells provide bonuses or impose penalties, the best bonus and worst penalty is applied from all Spells that affect the target. They do not stack.

Unless otherwise stated, you must have line of sight to your target.

rows.name: Touch Spells in Combat
textFields:
Certain Spells require you to touch the target. To touch a creature who does not wish to be touched, make an Opposed Melee (Brawling) or Sleight of Hand Test (generally Opposed by the target’s Dodge or Melee Skill) after making a successful Casting Test. If the Spell is a magic missile, reverse the Touch Test to determine the Hit Location struck.

Certain magical items, such as enchanted staffs, allow you to benefit from their reach when casting touch Spells. In this case, you may replace Melee (Brawling) or Sleight of Hand with an appropriate Melee Skill, such as Melee (Polearm) in the case of an enchanted staff. This Test is made purely to see if you touch the target with the item. It is not a separate attack that would inflict Damage in addition to the effects of the Spell.

rows.name: Channelling
textFields:
You can gather the magical energy needed to cast powerful Spells by channelling. To channel magic, you must decide which Wind of Magic you wish to channel and use your Action to make a Challenging (+0 SL) Channelling Test.

Each SL gathered through channelling adds to a pool of power. When you make a Casting Test for a spell of the appropriate Lore, you may add the SL gathered through channelling to the SL of your Casting Test. After making a Casting Test, all gathered power is lost. If you stop Channelling for any reason, you may make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test — if you fail, the power is lost.

rows.name: Critical and Fumbled Channelling
textFields:
Rolling a double on a successful Channelling Test adds an additional Willpower Bonus SL to your pool of power. If you fail and roll doubles, lose 1d10 SL and then roll on the Minor Miscast Table, adding +10 to the result for each SL of power lost.

If you take damage or suffer a Condition while channelling, you must make a Hard (-2 SL) Cool Test or lose 1d10 SL and roll on the Minor Miscast table, adding +10 per SL as above.

rows.name: Overcasting
textFields:
If a Casting Test generates SL beyond those required to cast a spell, you can spend the remaining SL on Overcasting. You can spend a number of SL equal to your Intelligence Bonus plus Willpower Bonus in this way.

•  Overcasting can add additional Range, Area of Effect, Duration, or Targets to the Spell. If the Spell is a magic missile, it can also add to the Damage. Spells may have additional options in their descriptions.

•  Spells with a Range of ‘You’ only ever target the spellcaster. Spells with a range of ‘Touch’ or a duration of ‘Instant’ or ‘Special’ may not be extended. Spells with no Area of Effect may not have their area increased.

•  Petty Spells cannot be Overcast.

### Overcast Table

| SL | Targets | Damage | Range | AoE | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | +1 | +1 Damage | ×2 | − | − |
| 2 | +1 | +2 Damage | ×2 | − | ×2 |
| 3 | +1 | +3 Damage | ×2 | ×2 | ×2 |
| 5 | +2 | +4 Damage | ×3 | ×2 | ×2 |
| 8 | +2 | +5 Damage | ×3 | ×2 | ×3 |
| 13 | +2 | +6 Damage | ×3 | ×2 | ×3 |
| 18+ | +3 | +7 Damage | ×4 | ×3 | ×3 |

rows.name: Second Sight
textFields: The Second Sight Talent allows you to perceive the Winds of Magic, and may use it to aid you in Perception, Track, or other Skill Tests where traces of the Winds of Magic might provide clues. A Character with the Second Sight Talent cannot simply turn it off, even should they wish to. In areas truly saturated by the Winds of Magic, they suffer Disadvantage on Perception Tests to perceive mundane phenomena.

rows.name: Armour Repels the Winds
textFields:
Metal and leather armour can make it harder for a spellcaster to control magical energy due to the fact that they attract Chamon (in the case of metal) or Ghur (in the case of leather). Spellcasters wearing armour suffer -1 SL to all Casting and Channelling Tests for every Armour Point on the Location with the most armour. Casters using Chamon may wear metal armour without penalty, and those using Ghur may wear leather armour without penalty. Armour Points granted by Spells do not repel the Spell’s Wind.

When creating a creature with the Spellcaster Trait or using a Magician Template (see Chapter 12: Bestiary), they typically eschew armour in order to make the most of their magical powers. Chaos sorcerers may wear Chaos Armour without penalty. Creatures granted an Armour Trait by their own scales or hide do not suffer penalties.

rows.name: Dispelling
textFields: Once per Round, you may attempt to dispel any Spell that targets a creature or point you can see within Willpower yards. Make an Opposed Language (Magick) Test against the spellcaster attempting to cast the Spell. If you win, the Spell is dispelled and has no effect. If the casting spellcaster wins the Opposed Test, use the SL for the Casting Test.

rows.name: Dispelling Persistent Spells
textFields:
You may attempt to dispel a Spell with a lasting effect as an Action. Make an Extended Challenging (+0 SL) Language (Magick) Test. When your SL reaches the CN of the ongoing Spell, it is dispelled.

Multiple spellcasters attempting to dispel the same Spell make Tests separately. If they know the same Lore of Magic, then they can provide Assistance instead. A spellcaster dispelling their own Spell receives +1 SL to the Language (Magick) Test.

rows.name: Grimoires
textFields:
Grimoires are books containing instructions on how to cast Spells. A typical grimoire contains notes of four Spells from the same Lore of Magic.

You may cast a Spell from a grimoire if the Spell belongs to a Lore of Magic that you possess. You need both hands free to flick through the pages. You cannot Overcast an unmemorised Spell; you need familiarity to modify it beyond the basics.

rows.name: Malignant Influences
textFields:
If you are subject to a Corrupting Influence and make a Casting Test or Channelling Test, there is an additional risk. Any time you would normally roll on the Minor Miscast Table, you must roll on the Major Miscast Table instead.

Spellcasters do not count as Malignant Influences in regard to their own Casting and Channelling Tests.

rows.name: Memorising Spells
textFields: You can memorise Spells by spending the amount of XP noted in the Petty Magic, Arcane Magic, and Chaos Magic Talents.

rows.name: Multiple Arcane Lores
textFields: An elf spellcaster may learn a number of Arcane Lores equal to their Willpower Bonus. An elf Character may not purchase a new Arcane Magic Talent until they have learned at least 8 Spells from the previous Lore. Any spellcaster may learn a

rows.name: Using Warpstone
textFields:
Some spellcasters prize warpstone as it can be used as a magical fuel. If you have a piece of warpstone, double any SL you generate on Casting Tests or Channelling Tests. Warpstone counts as a Malignant Influence as explained above.

When warpstone is used as a magical fuel, it is gradually consumed. Keep track of how many CN a particular piece of warpstone has provided. One gram of warpstone is consumed for every 20 CN of magical energy it provides.

In the Empire, the cults and various secular authorities take an extremely dim view of the use of warpstone, and those who possess or use it will be considered to be undertaking acts of Witchcraft even if they are licensed by a College of Magic. There is a thriving black market for the stuff if you possess the right contacts, though it is expensive. While all spellcasters might benefit from warpstone, skaven spellcasters use it as the primary source of their magical power. All Casting Tests and Channelling Tests made by skaven suffer from -4 SL unless they possess a piece of warpstone. The most accomplished skaven grey seers are experts in utilising warpstone, and do not count it as a Malignant Influence, though other skaven spellcasters do.

rows.name: Coin and Status
textFields:
Characters of a given Status most frequently use the coinage associated with their status.

•  Brass Tier: The poorest members of society are unlikely to see a gold coin in their lifetimes. They live humble lives, subsisting on plain foods and sleeping in shared rooms.

•  Silver Tier: The swelling middle classes may use pennies for ale and gold for major purchases, but shillings are their standard currency.

•  Gold Tier: The wealthiest elites rarely bother themselves with pennies, occasionally use silver to pay their underlings, and often enjoy the awe producing a gold coin can inspire in their social inferiors.

For GMs preferring hard numbers, spending around half your Status every day is usually enough to maintain appearances, though you may be living a little frugally. So, if you have a Status of Silver 4, spending at least 2 shillings per day will do for food and board, where if you have Brass 2 Status, you need only spend a pfennig a day.

rows.name: Money
textFields:
The Empire’s coins are usually minted in three denominations: brass pennies (d), silver shillings (/), and gold crowns (GC). Coins weigh around an ounce and, as their inherent value is determined by weight, even foreign coins can be easily valued with a set of scales, though they will likely draw a suspicious eye.

Standard coin values are: 1 gold crown (1 GC) = 20 silver shillings (20/–) = 240 brass pennies (240d) 1 silver shilling (1/–) = 12 brass pennies (12d) This is usually abbreviated to: 1 GC = 20/– = 240d

rows.name: Availability
textFields:
All Trappings have an Availability: either Common, Scarce, Rare, or Exotic.

Common items are found in almost every corner of the Empire and are always assumed to be readily available.

Scarce and Rare items are less common, and you need to pass an Availability Test to find any locally in stock; the chance of passing the Test depends upon the settlement size.

Exotic items are exceedingly rare, and only available if the GM says so, or if you commission the item from an appropriate artisan (perhaps with a Commission Endeavour, see page 197), or make it yourself (perhaps with a Crafting Endeavour, see page 198).

Once you know an item’s Availability, check it on the following table to see if it is in stock.

| Availability | Village | Town | City |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Common | In stock! | In stock! | In stock! |
| Scarce | 30% | 60% | 90% |
| Rare | 15% | 30% | 45% |
| Exotic | Not in stock | Not in stock | Not in stock |

If you fail an Availability Test for Scarce or Rare items, you can either reroll when you arrive at a new settlement or you can try again next week if the settlement is Town-size or larger.

• The GM may overrule Availability as dictated by local details. For example, basic rowboats are automatically available if the adventure is located in a fishing village that features a renowned boat-builder.

• Availability percentages can be increased by +10% or +20% if you are especially diligent, belong to a relevant Career such as Merchant or Fence, or spend an entire day shopping and making Gossip Tests.

rows.name: Clipping
textFields: Embezzlers can trim slivers of precious metal away from the edges of coins. This scam is called ‘clipping’ or ‘shaving’ and is practised mainly by shopkeepers or tollkeepers who have access to large quantities of other peoples’ money. Gold and silver filings are then melted down and sold to jewellers, counterfeiters, or fences. Clipped coins can be detected with the Evaluate Skill; the more clipped the coin, the easier the Test.

rows.name: Counterfeiting
textFields:
The diversity of coinage circulating the Empire means counterfeiting is rife. Reiklanders may be accustomed to seeing coins from other provinces, but are always wary of being scammed.

A successful Evaluate Test will detect counterfeit coins, typically by inspecting coins for weight and hardness.

Actually producing counterfeit coins is much harder. It requires an Art (Engraving) Test to carve a convincing stamping die, then a Trade (Smith) Test to strike the coins, usually with the aid of an assistant. Including a higher precious metal content makes Evaluate Tests to detect counterfeits more difficult; using less than a fifth makes it much easier to spot the fake coins.

rows.name: Going to Market
textFields: Once you start play, the availability of rarer goods is restricted. A village market may only have a few locally sourced goods for sale, whilst the emporiums and market squares of the Empire’s cities may contain all manner of exotic fare.

rows.name: Bargaining and Trading
textFields:
People of the Empire love a good bargain, and eager shoppers fill town squares looking for the best deals. When buying goods, there are two primary Skills to Test: Evaluate and Haggle.

Evaluate is used to identify the quality of an item (see Craftsmanship below). Vendors can use Evaluate to appraise coins for their exchange value, or spot counterfeits. Anyone can also use Evaluate to estimate the prices of Rare or Exotic items.

Haggle is used by buyers and sellers, typically in Opposed Tests. Haggling is expected and most prices are marked up to account for this. See page 143 for the effects of using the Haggle Skill.

rows.name: Bartering
textFields: Rural and mercantile commerce often involves trading one commodity for another without exchanging money. Some folks see this as a preferable and more honest form of exchange that does away with the risk of fraudulent currency and unwelcome taxation. If you wish to barter one or more items for something of roughly equivalent value, note the Availability of the rarest item involved in the transaction. Halve this value, rounding down, and roll to see if you’ve found someone wiling to partake in the trade. If successful, the deal goes ahead, though players may make a Haggle Test if they want to argue for more favourable terms. It is up to the GM if anyone is willing to make a particular trade — looted hand weapons may be of limited use to a boat builder, for example.

rows.name: Craftsmanship
textFields:
The items available in the shops, stalls, and merchant halls of the Empire vary significantly in quality. Not everything is made equal, and the Craftsmanship rules reflect this using Item Qualities and Item Flaws.

An Item Quality makes the trapping a little better, but harder to find. An Item Flaw makes the trapping a little worse, but easier to find.

rows.name: Item Qualities
textFields: A Trapping is called a Quality Trapping if it has more Item Qualities than Flaws.

rows.name: Lowering the Price
textFields:
If you cannot find a buyer, you can try lowering the price. Each time you halve the money you are willing to accept, the Availability of a buyer increases by one step.

Example: Corporal Schütze has fled his State Army regiment with a stolen Hochland Long Rifle, and is keen to sell. As it is an Exotic item, there are no immediate buyers he can find on the street. The GM determines the base price Schütze can expect is half the weapon’s value (so 50 GC), so Schütze decides to drop the price by half two times, saying he will accept 12 GC 10/–, which increases the Availability of a buyer two steps from Exotic to Scarce.

rows.name: Selling
textFields:
Selling your Trappings during desperate times, or simply offloading loot, is handled in exactly the same fashion as buying, but this time you will be making money, not spending it. So, you first check for Availability of a buyer in the same fashion as checking for stock. You then bargain and trade, with Evaluate Tests and Haggle Tests as the GM prefers, and finally you set a price. Typically, the base cost when selling is half the item’s listed price, meaning, when selling second-hand, you usually make between a quarter to half an item’s worth after Haggling.

If you put time into Gossip Tests and wandering the local town, you might find someone willing to pay up to 80% of the item’s listed value, though that is left in the hands of the GM.

rows.name: Beasts of Burden
textFields: Encumbrance Points for draft animals and vehicles like mules, horses, carts, and wagons are listed in their descriptions. Each human-sized passenger is assumed to weigh around 10 Encumbrance Points, modified by the GM as necessary.

rows.name: Encumbrance
textFields:
Even the doughtiest Dwarf cannot carry a limitless number of Trappings. To help you track how much you are carrying, all items are marked as weighing a number of Encumbrance Points (sometimes abbreviated to ‘Enc’), typically from 0–3, where 0 shows a trifling item that is easily carried, and 3 represents something that is a struggle to heft. The number of Encumbrance Points you can carry without penalty is determined by your Strength Bonus + Toughness Bonus. Thus, average Humans begin play able to carry around 6 Encumbrance Points.

### Encumbrance Examples

| Enc | Example Trappings |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Knives, coins, jewellery |
| 1 | Sword, mandolin, sling bag |
| 2 | Bastard sword, tent, backpack |
| 3 | Halberd, cask, large sack |

### Small Items

Common sense usually dictates the number of smaller items someone can carry before becoming Encumbered. To provide a rough guide, money weighs 1 Encumbrance Point per 200 coins.

### Oversized Items

Certain large items weigh 4 or more Encumbrance Points, such as barrels or saddlebags. You may normally only carry one oversized object, and it likely requires both hands.

### Beasts of Burden

Encumbrance Points for draft animals and vehicles like mules, horses, carts, and wagons are listed in their descriptions. Each human-sized passenger is assumed to weigh around 10 Encumbrance Points, modified by the GM as necessary.

### Worn Items

Worn items like armour and clothing have their Encumbrance reduced by 1, often counting as Encumbrance 0 when worn.

### Overburdened

Characters who exceed their Encumbrance capacity are slowed and prone to fatigue. Movement reduction and Travel Fatigue incurred from Encumbrance stacks with any Armour penalties. Endurance Tests to resist the Fatigued Condition incur Disadvantage while Overburdened.

### Overburdened Examples

| Enc | Penalty |
| --- | --- |
| Up to limit | No penalties |
| Up to double limit | −1 Movement (min. 3), −10 Agility, +1 Travel Fatigue |
| Up to triple limit | −2 Movement (min. 2), −20 Agility (min. 10), +2 Travel Fatigue |
| More than 3× | You are unable to move |

### Encumbrance and Attributes

Movement and Agility penalties for Encumbrance are applied immediately and can only be removed by dropping equipment.

### Encumbrance and Travel Fatigue

Fatigued Conditions are accrued at the end of a day’s travel and can only be removed with a long rest.

rows.name: Encumbrance and Attributes
textFields: Movement and Agility penalties for Encumbrance are applied immediately and can only be removed by dropping equipment.

rows.name: Encumbrance and Travel Fatigue
textFields: Fatigued Conditions are accrued at the end of a day’s travel and can only be removed with a long rest.

rows.name: Item Flaws
textFields:
A Trapping is called a Flawed Trapping if it has more Item Flaws than Qualities. Each Flaw halves the listed price and improves Availability by one step. Many vendors sell Flawed items, but pretend they are anything but. A successful Test with any appropriate Skill — such as Evaluate, or Melee for weapons, or Trade for tools — will spot such underhanded activities.

Note: Exotic items do not have their Availability modified by being Flawed — they are always difficult to find, even shoddy examples.

Example: A suit of plate armour that is both Bulky and Unreliable costs a quarter of the list price, and raises Availability from Rare to Common.

rows.name: Overburdened
textFields:
Characters who exceed their Encumbrance capacity are slowed and prone to fatigue. Movement reduction and Travel Fatigue incurred from Encumbrance stacks with any Armour penalties. Endurance Tests to resist the Fatigued Condition incur Disadvantage while Overburdened.

| Enc | Penalty |
| --- | --- |
| Up to limit | No penalties |
| Up to double limit | −1 Movement (min. 3), −10 Agility, +1 Travel Fatigue |
| Up to triple limit | −2 Movement (min. 2), −20 Agility (min. 10), +2 Travel Fatigue |
| More than 3× | You are unable to move |

rows.name: Oversized Items
textFields: Certain large items weigh 4 or more Encumbrance Points, such as barrels or saddlebags. You may normally only carry one oversized object, and it likely requires both hands.

rows.name: Small Items
textFields: Common sense usually dictates the number of smaller items someone can carry before becoming Encumbered. To provide a rough guide, money weighs 1 Encumbrance Point per 200 coins.

rows.name: Worn Items
textFields: Worn items like armour and clothing have their Encumbrance reduced by 1, often counting as Encumbrance 0 when worn.

rows.name: Cavalry
textFields: Cavalry weapons are assumed to be used when mounted. When on foot, all two-handed weapons in the Cavalry Weapon Group also count as Two-handed weapons. Single-handed Cavalry weapons count as Improved Weapons when unmounted unless otherwise stated.

rows.name: Fencing
textFields: Those with Melee (Basic) can use Fencing weapons, but cannot use their Weapon Qualities.

rows.name: Flail
textFields: Unskilled Characters add the Dangerous Weapon Flaw.

rows.name: Melee Weapon Groups
textFields: All melee weapons are assigned to a Weapon Group. Each Weapon Group requires a separate Skill to master its use. So, Melee (Flail) allows you to use Flails and is a separate Skill from Melee (Polearm), which allows you to use Polearms. If you use a weapon from a Group where you have no Advances, you Test your Weapon Skill to hit with the weapon. While you still suffer all the weapon’s Flaws, you cannot use any of its Qualities. Some Melee Weapon Groups also have special rules.

rows.name: Weapon Reach
textFields:
The lengths of the weapons are progressively bigger as follows.

•  Personal: Your legs and fists, perhaps your head, and anything attached to those

•  Very Short: Less than a foot in length

•  Short: Up to 2 feet in length

•  Average: Up to 3 feet long

•  Long: Up to 6 foot long

•  Very Long: Up to 10 feet in length; can Engage enemies up to 4 yards away, rather than just 2

•  Massive: Anything over 10 feet long; can Engage enemies up to 6 yards away, rather than just 2

rows.name: Weapon Reach and Defence
textFields: If your weapon is longer than your opponent’s, you benefit from +1 SL to defensive Melee Tests as you find it easier to keep them at bay.

rows.name: Blackpowder and Explosives
textFields: Those with Ranged (Engineering) can use Blackpowder and Explosive weapons without penalty.

rows.name: Crossbows and Throwing
textFields: Crossbows and Throwing weapons are relatively simple to use. You can use Crossbow and Throwing weapons with Ballistic Skill, but Ballistic Skill Tests suffer from –1 SL.

rows.name: Engineering
textFields: You can use all Engineering weapons with Ranged (Blackpowder), but Ranged (Blackpowder) Tests suffer from a penalty of –2 SL.

rows.name: Ranged Weapon Groups
textFields:
Ranged weapons are difficult to master. You cannot attempt a Ranged Test for a weapon you do not have the correct speciality for.

So, if you know Ranged (Blackpowder), you cannot attempt a Ranged (Bow) Test. However, there are a few exceptions.

rows.name: Weapon Range
textFields:
A weapon’s range is its Medium range in yards. Chapter 5: Rules presents modifiers if a weapon is at Point Blank, Short, Long, or Extreme range. Calculate ranges as follows:

### Calculating Range Bands

| Band | Range |
| --- | --- |
| Point Blank | 4 yards |
| Short | Range ÷ 2 |
| Medium | Listed weapon range |
| Long | Range × 2 |
| Extreme | Range × 3 |

### Example Weapon Ranges

| Weapon | Point Blank | Short | Medium | Long | Extreme |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bow | 4 | 25 | 50 | 100 | 150 |
| Hochland Long Rifle | 4 | 50 | 100 | 200 | 300 |
| Pistol | 4 | 10 | 20 | 40 | 60 |
| Sling | 4 | 20 | 40 | 80 | 120 |

rows.name: Armour
textFields:
‘Straps tight! A secure helm is the difference between the armourers fixing a dent and me having to find some poor sod to replace you.’ – Sergeant Hubrecht Grünner, Schilderheim Militia Leader

Armour is listed in the following format:

•  Armour Type: Each armour is listed by type.

•  Price: The price to buy an average piece of the armour.

•  Enc: The Encumbrance for the armour.

•  Availability: The Availability of the armour.

•  Penalty: Any penalty for wearing that specific piece of Armour in addition to those opposed by Encumbrance (page 299). Note: Some armour brings a penalty if you wear any of it, such as wearing any chain brings a penalty of –1 SL to Stealth Tests.

•  Locations: The Hit Locations the Armour protects.

•  AP: The number of Armour Points the armour provides to the protected Hit Locations.

•  Qualities and Flaws: Any Armour Qualities or Flaws the armour may possess.

rows.name: Armour and Size
textFields: Armour gets heavier and more expensive the larger the creature it is made for. For each step above Size (Average), a piece of armour gains +1 Encumbrance and doubles in price. Conversely, for each step below Size (Average), subtract –1 Encumbrance and halve the price.

rows.name: Creatures and Equipment
textFields:
Melee weapons are listed in a creature’s attacks showing the weapon’s name, its Skill with that weapon and the total Damage it inflicts (the creature’s Strength Bonus is included) in parentheses, followed by any Qualities or Flaws in italics. For example, a spear-armed creature would have: Spear (30/+7) Impale.

Ranged weapons are listed with the weapon and ammunition it uses, followed by parentheses containing the creature’s Skill with that weapon and the total Damage it inflicts (appropriate Strength Bonus is included), its range in yards, and any Qualities or Flaws in italics. For example, a creature armed with a Bow and Arrows would have: Bow and Arrows (30/+7) 50 yards, Impale.

Many creatures are armed with teeth, claws, horns, or other natural weaponry as their primary weapon. Unless otherwise mentioned, the Reach of such weapons is Personal and they possess no Qualities or Flaws.

Where an Armour value is provided, the total Toughness Bonus + Armour Points is shown in parentheses.

Armour and Weapons given to bipedal creatures with hands are just suggestions. If the GM wishes, such creatures could be armed and armoured with anything from the Consumer Guide, and can be assumed to have any Skills they need to use the items without penalty.

rows.name: Customising Creatures
textFields:
The information presented is for the basic example of each particular individual. You can adapt these entries for variety, or to create more powerful creatures, by changing their Characteristics and adding Skills, Talents, and Creature Traits. The quickest way to create fast NPC adversaries is to use Creature Traits; all creatures come with one or more Creature Traits as standard, but additional ones can be added as required. The listed Optional Traits for a creature present common variants of the species, but you can apply any Trait to any creature if it fits your game. See page 356 for Creature Traits.

The templates on page 353 are a quick way of creating a variety of opponents from more organised species or societies. Apply the template to the basic information for the species to create a Soldier, Skirmisher, Elite, Leader, Commander, Spellcaster, or Spellcaster Lord. You could even use the Career system to develop well rounded and, depending on how much XP you decide to spend on them, terrifyingly powerful allies or antagonists.

rows.name: Individual Characteristic Advances
textFields:
Characteristic and Skill Advances are bought in +5 increments. However, in some cases, a player might want to purchase individual Advances. This might be because they just need a point or two to get to a Characteristic to a round number and thus increase their Characteristic Bonus, or because they prefer frequent modest improvements over larger jumps in ability.

Use the table below to determine the XP cost for individual Advances. Once you switch to this method, you need to have bought a number Advances that is a multiple of 5 if you wish to return to the method presented on page 191.

| Advances | Characteristic: cost per +1 | Skills: cost per +1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 to 5 | 25 | 10 |
| 6 to 10 | 35 | 15 |
| 11 to 15 | 50 | 20 |
| 16 to 20 | 70 | 30 |
| 21 to 25 | 100 | 50 |
| 26 to 30 | 140 | 80 |
| 31 to 35 | 190 | 120 |
| 36 to 40 | 260 | 170 |
| 41 to 45 | 360 | 170 |
| 46 to 50 | 510 | 340 |
| 51 to 55 | 720 | 500 |
| 56 to 60 | 1005 | 700 |
| 61 to 65 | 1390 | 950 |
| 66 to 70 | 1800 | 1300 |
| 71+ | 2250 | 1700 |

rows.name: Afraid
textFields: The creature gains Fear of the Target. When encountered, they must make an Extended Psychology Test (page 183). Until their SL equals or exceeds the Targetâ€™s Fear Rating, the creature cannot gain Momentum, and Melee Attacks made against them by the Target benefit from Advantage. See page 183 for Fear rules.

rows.name: Amphibious
textFields: The creature is as at home in water as they are on land. They have the Swim Skill, add +1 SL to all Swim Tests, and move at full Movement through water.

rows.name: Animosity
textFields: The creature dislikes the Target. When the creature encounters the object of its Animosity, make a Psychology Test (page 183). On a failure, it must attack the target socially or physically, as appropriate, gaining +1 SL on Fellowship based Tests to oppose or disparage them. See page 183 for full Animosity rules.

rows.name: Belligerent
textFields: The creature loves to win a fight. As long as they possess Momentum, they are immune to Fear.

rows.name: Bestial
textFields: The creature has no rational thought or language. It shies away from fire and gains a Broken Condition if struck and wounded by it. In defence, it only uses the Dodge Skill. If it loses more than half its Wounds, it will attempt to Flee unless protecting its young or cornered, or unless it has the Territorial Trait. If so, it enters Frenzy (see page 184).

rows.name: Bite
textFields: The creature may lose Momentum to make a Free Attack. The Damage equals Rating and includes their Strength Bonus already. Free Attack - Weapon Skill or Ballistic Skill attack that does not use your Action on your Turn.

rows.name: Blessed
textFields: The creature can enact Blessings, the relevant deity is indicated in parentheses. A creature with this Trait has a Pray Skill at Fel + 10 (or more at the GMâ€™s discretion).

rows.name: Bounce
textFields: The creature can bounce high, perhaps with powerful limbs, magic, or stubby wings. When Charging, Leaping, or Sprinting, they double their Movement Attribute and can ignore all intervening terrain and creatures as they leap over them.

rows.name: Breath
textFields: The creatureâ€™s breath is a powerful weapon. As a ranged attack, they can activate their Breath as a Free Attack, targeting 1 creature they can see within 20 + Toughness Bonus yards and all creatures within SB yards of that target. The attacker makes an Opposed Ballistic Skill/Dodge Test against all targets (the attacker's single roll Opposed by each individual target). If a creature without a BS makes a Breath Attack, count it as having a BS of 30. Losing targets take Rating Damage. Further, if the Trait has any of the following Types in parentheses, apply the associated rules. 0 Acid: Inflicts Damage of TB +4. All weapons and armour carried by the targets suffer 1 Damage. 0 Cold: Inflicts Damage of SB +2. Targets gain a Fatigued Condition; until they lose the Condition, their weapons gain the Slow Flaw. 0 Electricity: Inflicts Damage of SB +2. Damage ignores metal armour. Targets gain a Stunned Condition. 0 Fire: Inflicts Damage of SB +3. Targets gain an Ablaze Condition. 0 Poison: Inflicts Damage of TB +2. Targets gain a Poisoned Condition. 0 Smoke: The area fills with smoke, blocking line of sight and causing Suffocation (page 169) for Toughness Bonus Rounds. The creature is immune to their own Breath. This attack is Magical.

rows.name: Champion
textFields: The creature is an extraordinarily skilled warrior. If they win an Opposed Test when defending in melee combat, they can cause Damage just as if they were the attacker.

rows.name: Chill Grasp
textFields: The creatureâ€™s touch chills their enemiesâ€™ souls. If they lose Momentum, then for their Action, they can attempt an Opposed Weapon Skill/Dodge or Melee Test. If they win, the target loses 1d10 + SL Wounds ignoring Toughness Bonus and Armour Points. This attack is Magical.

rows.name: Cold-blooded
textFields: The creature is cold-blooded and slow to react. They gain Advantage to Cool Tests. If they gain the Surprised Condition, this Condition is not lost the first time it should be (typically at the end of the Round or if they are attacked).

rows.name: Constrictor
textFields: The creature can squeeze and crush their prey. Any successful hit gives the target an Entangled Condition. The creature may then enter a Grapple if they wish (see page 167).

rows.name: Construct
textFields: The creature is a construct of magic, quite mindless, and bound together with enchantments. It has no Intelligence, Willpower, or Fellowship Characteristics, and need never Test them. If it is ever called upon to Test based on Willpower, use Toughness instead. If it has no spellcaster controlling it, or does not possess the Territorial Trait, it wanders mindlessly. For the purpose of calculating its Wounds, use its Strength Bonus whenever Willpower Bonus is required. All its attacks are Magical.

rows.name: Corrosive Blood
textFields: The creatureâ€™s blood is corrosive. Every time they are wounded, blood splashes free and all targets Engaged with them take 1d10 Damage (roll once and apply to all targets).

rows.name: Corruption
textFields: The creature is tainted by Chaos, or perhaps suffused with Dark Magics. They are a Corrupting Influence with a Strength marked in parentheses. See page 187.

rows.name: Daemonic
textFields: The creatureâ€™s essence is raw magic, and unholy ichor pumps through what passes for their veins. Daemonic creatures do not require the normal prerequisites for life such as food, water, air, and so on. All their attacks are Magical. Roll 1d10 after any blow is received, if the creature rolls Rating or higher, the blow is ignored, even if it is a Critical. They may not use this ability to ignore Magical blows such as those caused by creatures with the Magical Trait or weapons with the Magical Quality. Should the creature be reduced to 0 Wounds, their soul returns to the Realms of Chaos immediately, removing them from play.

rows.name: Dark Vision
textFields: The creature can see in the dark as if it were daylight.

rows.name: Disease
textFields: The creature carries the disease listed, though whether they suffer from the disease is up to the GM. Others will have to Test as appropriate for Contraction (see page 179).

rows.name: Distracting
textFields: The creature distracts or confuses foes, possibly exuding a soporific musk or nauseating reek, or through its bizarre and horrifying appearance. All living targets within a number of yards equal to the creatureâ€™s Toughness Bonus suffer a -2 SL penalty to all Tests. A target can only suffer this penalty once, no matter how many Distracting foes there are.

rows.name: Ethereal
textFields: The creatureâ€™s form is insubstantial, allowing them to pass through solid objects. They can only be harmed by Magical attacks and all their attacks are Magical.

rows.name: Fear
textFields: The creature causes supernatural Fear in other creatures. Opponents must make an Extended Psychology Test (page 183). Until they have accumulated more SL than the creatureâ€™s Fear Rating (1, if not stated), they cannot gain Momentum, and melee attacks against them benefit from Advantage. See page 183 for Fear rules.

rows.name: Fly
textFields: As the creatureâ€™s Move, they can fly up to Rating yards. When flying, they ignore all intervening terrain, obstacles, or creatures. At the end of the move, they decide whether they have landed or are still flying. They can use this move to Charge. If they start their turn flying, they must choose to Fly for their Move. If they cannot do this, the GM decides how far the creature falls (see page 169). When targeting them, measure horizontal distance as normal, then increase range by 1 step. So, a Long Range shot would become Extreme Range, and if they were at Extreme Range, they could not be shot at all. When flying, they suffer a -20 penalty to Ranged Attacks as they swoop and wheel in the sky.

rows.name: Frenzy
textFields: The creature may make a Willpower Test to enter a Frenzy (page 184). While Frenzied, they are immune to Psychology, cannot flee or retreat, must attack the nearest visible enemy, gain a Free Attack each Round, +1 Damage, and may only attack or move to attack. Frenzy ends when no enemies remain in sight, or if the creature becomes Stunned or Unconscious. Afterwards, they gain a Fatigued Condition.

rows.name: Ghostly Howl
textFields: The creature can emit a hideous scream, capable of killing those who hear it. Once per turn, this creature can lose their Momentum to unleash a howl as a Free Attack. All living targets within a number of yards equal to the creatureâ€™s Strength who can hear it immediately gain 3 Deafened Conditions and suffer 1d10 Wounds ignoring Toughness Bonus and Armour Points. Those affected must also pass an Average (+2 SL) Cool Test or gain a Broken Condition. This attack is Magical.

rows.name: Grim
textFields: The creature is incredibly lethal, able to quickly gain the upper hand over almost any opponent. At the end of its turn, if the creature does not have Momentum (page 167), it gains it.

rows.name: Hatred
textFields: When the creature encounters the Target, they must make a Psychology Test (page 183). On a failure, they become subject to Hatred. While Hatred lasts, they must attack the hated foe by the fastest and most deadly means possible, gain +1 SL on Melee and Ranged Tests against them, and are immune to Intimidate and Fear (but not Terror) caused by the Target. See page 184 for full Hatred rules.

rows.name: Horns
textFields: The creature has horns or some other sharp appendage (if their Horns Trait represents a different feature, it will be noted in parentheses). When the creature charges into combat, they may make a Free Attack with their Horns, with a Damage of SB +4.

rows.name: Hungry
textFields: The creature is always hungry for fresh meat. If they kill or incapacitate a living opponent (or encounter a fresh body), they must pass an Average (+2 SL) Cool Test or feast, losing their next Move and Action.

rows.name: Immune to Psychology
textFields: Whether brave, stupid, or just caught up in the moment, the creature is utterly stoic. They ignore the Psychology rules (see page 183).

rows.name: Immunity
textFields: The creature is completely immune to a certain type of harm, such as poison, magic, or electricity. All harm of that type, including from a Critical Wound, is ignored.

rows.name: Infected
textFields: The creature, or their weapon, carries a nasty infection. If they cause a living opponent to lose Wounds, the opponent must pass an Easy (+4 SL) Endurance Test or contract a Festering Wound (see page 180).

rows.name: Infestation
textFields: The creatureâ€™s hide is infested with biting fleas or similar. All opponents suffer a penalty of -1 SL to hit them in melee combat as the parasites distract and overwhelm them.

rows.name: Magic Resistance
textFields: The creature is resistant to magic. Any Casting Test to cast a Spell that would affect them suffers -3 SL. No creature with this Trait may possess the Channelling Skill or the Arcane Magic, Bless, Chaos Magic, Invoke, Petty Magic, or Witch! Talents, and vice versa.

rows.name: Magical
textFields: The creature is wreathed in magic. Their attacks count as Magical, and they can harm creatures only susceptible to Magical attacks.

rows.name: Many Heads
textFields: The creature has more than one head. If a Critical Wound affecting the head stuns, kills, or renders the creature unconscious it will only affect the creature once all the heads are either disabled or affected to a similar degree. If the creature has the Bite, Horns, or Tongue Traits it can make a number of Free Attacks equal to the number of healthy heads. The creature benefits from +2 SL to Perception Tests whilst it has at least two healthy heads.

rows.name: Mark of Chaos
textFields: One of the dark powers has marked this creature with a physical brand, proclaiming it one of their favoured servants. The exact effects of this mark depend on which of the Chaos gods bestowed the Mark. Khorne: The creature benefits from the Frenzy Talent. This creature gains the Etiquette (Followers of Khorne) Talent and is subject to Animosity towards overt followers of Slaanesh. The creature is also subject to Animosity by followers of Slaanesh, so long as the Mark of Khorne is visible. The Character may not use the Language (Magick) or Channelling skills unless it is to dispel a spell. Additionally, they may purchase the following Talents as if they were Career Advances for the normal XP costs: Berserk Charge, Combat Aware, Combat Reflexes, Furious Assault, Implacable, Magic Resistance, Resistance (Magic), Resolute, Strike Mighty Blow, Warrior Born. Nurgle: The creature benefits from a bonus of +10 to its Toughness. This creature gains the Etiquette (Followers of Nurgle) Talent and is subject to Animosity towards overt followers of Tzeentch. The creature is also subject to Animosity by followers of Tzeentch, so long as the Mark of Nurgle is visible. Additionally they may purchase the following Talents as if they were Career Advances for the normal XP costs: Frightening, Hardy, Implacable, Iron Jaw, Menacing, Resistance (Poison), Resistance (Disease), Robust, Tenacious, and Very Resilient. Slaanesh: The creature gains the Fearless (Everything) Talent. This creature gains the Etiquette (Followers of Slaanesh) Talent and is subject to Animosity towards overt followers of Khorne. The creature is also subject to Animosity by followers of Khorne, so long as the Mark of Slaanesh is visible. Additionally, they may purchase the following Talents as if they were Career Advances for the normal XP costs: Attractive, Blather, Careful Strike, Combat Master, Gregarious, Inspiring, Lightning Reflexes, Nimblefingered, Resistant (Poison), and Sharp. Tzeentch: This creature gains 1d10/3 Mutations (rounding up), alternating between Mental and Physical Mutations. This creature gains Etiquette (Followers of Tzeentch), and is subject to Animosity towards overt followers of Nurgle. The creature is also subject to Animosity by followers of Nurgle, so long as the Mark of Tzeentch can be seen. Additionally, this creature may purchase the following Talents as if they were Career Advances: Aethyric Attunement, Arcane Magic (Any), Chaos Magic (Tzeentch), Fast Hands, Instinctive Diction, Magical Sense, Petty Magic, Second Sight, War Wizard, and Witch! for the normal XP costs.

rows.name: Mental Corruption
textFields: The creature has Chaos on the mind. Roll on the Mental Corruption Table found on page 189.

rows.name: Miracles
textFields: The creature can enact Miracles; the relevant deity is indicated in parentheses. A creature with this Trait has a Pray Skill at Fel + 10 (or more at the GMâ€™s discretion).

rows.name: Mutation
textFields: The creature bears a Mutation. Roll on the Physical Corruption Table found on page 189.

rows.name: Night Vision
textFields: The creature can see very well in natural darkness. They can see clearly in such darkness for 20 yards and can extend the effective illumination distance of any light sources by a further 20 yards.

rows.name: Painless
textFields: The creature is impervious to pain. All non-amputation penalties suffered from Critical Wounds are ignored, although Conditions are suffered as normal.

rows.name: Petrifying Gaze
textFields: The creatureâ€™s gaze can turn flesh to stone. As an Action, the creature may lose its Momentum to unleash its petrifying gaze against one living target it can see. The creature makes a Ballistic Skill Test, opposed by the targetâ€™s Initiative. If the creature wins, it inflicts a Stunned Condition, and one more for each SL after the first. If they win by 6+ SL, the target is permanently turned to stone. If the target is a spellcaster, they can oppose the Test with Language (Magick) instead of Initiative.

rows.name: Regeneration
textFields: The creature can heal at an extraordinary rate, even regrowing severed parts. At the start of each Round, if they have more than 0 Wounds remaining, they automatically regenerate 1d10 Wounds. If they have 0 Wounds remaining, they regenerate a single Wound on a 1d10 roll of 8+. If they ever roll a 10 for regenerating, they also fully regenerate a Critical Wound, losing all penalties and Conditions associated with it. Any Wounds or Critical Wounds caused by fire may not be regenerated.

rows.name: Size
textFields:
This Trait represents creatures whose size differs from the game standard (i.e. roughly human-sized). There are five steps of Size, ranging from Tiny to Monstrous. Size Examples Butterfly, Mouse, Pigeon, Cat, Hawk, Tiny Human Infant Giant Rat, Halfling, Human Child, Average Dwarf, Elf, Human Large Horse, Ogre, Troll Enormous Griffon, Wyvern, Manticore Monstrous Dragon, Giant, Greater Daemon Size Combat Modifiers Large creatures do more Damage when they land a hit. These modifiers donâ€™t apply to Ranged Attacks or extra attacks. NPC profiles already include these modifiers. 
â€¢ Small: Damage as normal 
â€¢ Average: Damage as normal 
â€¢ Large: Damage as normal plus additional SB Damage 
â€¢ Enormous: Damage as normal plus additional SB Damage 
â€¢ Monstrous: Damage as normal plus additional (2 x SB) Damage Defending Against Big Creatures When fighting a creature of larger size, you suffer a penalty of -2 SL when using Melee to defend in an Opposed Test. It is better to dodge a giant swinging a tree trunk than try to parry it! Fear Agressive creatures cause Fear in those smaller than them. Moving in Combat Creatures ignore the need to Disengage from melee combat with smaller combatants. Opposed Strength During Opposed Strength Tests (and similar), if one creature is 2 or more Size steps larger, they win automatically. If one creature is 1 Size step larger, the smaller creature must score a Critical to contest the roll. If they do, SL are compared as normal. All other results mean the larger creature wins. Outnumbering Larger Creatures Larger creatures count as several creatures for the sake of working out if they are outnumbered in combat. 
â€¢ Small: Counts as 1 creature 
â€¢ Average: Counts as 1 creature 
â€¢ Large: Counts as 2 creatures 
â€¢ Enormous: Counts as 3 creatures 
â€¢ Monstrous: Counts as 4 creatures So, you would need 4 Size (Average) creatures to outnumber a Size (Large) creature by 2 to 1, or 3 Size (Large) creatures to outnumber a Size (Monstrous) creature by 2 to 1. Conversely, for the sake of larger opponents being daunting enough, they do not themselves count as multiple opponents when working out if they receive a bonus for outnumbering themselves. 2 Size (Large) Ogres outnumber 1 Size (Average) Human 2 to 1, not 4 to 1. Creatures that are larger than their opponents may lose Momentum to make one Stomp as a Free Attack, kicking downwards or otherwise bashing smaller opponents out of the way. This attack has a Damage equal to their Strength Bonus and uses Melee (Brawling). Larger creatures have more Wounds: Size Wounds Small 2 Ã— Toughness Bonus Strength Bonus + (2 Ã— Toughness Average Bonus) + Willpower Bonus (Strength Bonus + (2 Ã— Toughness Large Bonus) + Willpower Bonus) Ã— 2 (Strength Bonus + (2 Ã— Toughness Enormous Bonus) + Willpower Bonus) Ã— 4 (Strength Bonus + (2 Ã— Toughness Monstrous Bonus) + Willpower Bonus) Ã— 8 ADJUSTING A CREATUREâ€™S SIZE if you wish to use Size to make a creature bigger then increase Strength and Toughness by +10 and reduce Agility by -5 per step of size you increase the creature. reverse this if you wish to make a creature smaller. Example: The Giant Spider described in the Bestiary is Size (Small) with a Strength of 15, Toughness of 25, and an Agility of 35. If it were made Size (Large) it would have a Strength of 35, Toughness of 45, and Agility of 25. Its Wounds would increase to 26, its fangs would inflict +5 Damage and its Bite would increase to +6 Damage.

rows.name: Skittish
textFields: The creature is scared by spectacular visible effects of magic or noises such as thunderclaps or explosions. If such occurs, they receive +3 Broken Conditions.

rows.name: Spellcaster
textFields: The creature can cast spells; the specific Lore(s) of Magic are indicated in parentheses. Add the Spellcaster or Spellcaster Lord template or, if that wouldnâ€™t be appropriate, add Channelling (Choose a Wind) (WP +10) and Language (Magick) (Int + 10) as if they were Basic Skills. The GM may increase the numbers of skills if they deem it appropriate.

rows.name: Sprinter
textFields: The creature has a long stride, perhaps because it is a quadruped or has especially long legs. Multiply Run Movement by 1.5 when Running.

rows.name: Stealthy
textFields: The creature is especially stealthy. They are granted the Stealth (Rural) Skill at Ag +10. This number may be increased at the GMâ€™s discretion.

rows.name: Striding Gait
textFields: The creature is at home in the listed terrain. They suffer no penalties for moving through the listed terrain and add +1 SL to Athletics and Stealth Tests in the listed terrain.

rows.name: Stupid
textFields: While not devoid of self-awareness (and so lacking the Bestial Trait), the creature is stupid. If they are near any allies without the Stupid Trait, they guide them and nothing happens. Otherwise, they must pass an Easy (+4 SL) Intelligence Test at the start of each Round or become very confused. Should this occur, they will drool, perhaps sitting down or picking their nose, doing little of use, losing both their Move and Action for that Turn.

rows.name: Swarm
textFields: Swarms are large numbers of the same creature acting as one. The swarm counts as a single creature that ignores the Psychology rules (see page 183), and can ignore the Engaged rules when using its Move. All opponents Engaged with a Swarm automatically lose 1 Wound at the end of every Round as the Swarm overwhelms anything close. The Swarm has five times the Wounds of a normal example of the creature and gains +10 Weapon Skill. Any attempts to shoot the Swarm gain a +40 bonus to hit. Swarms ignore all the Size Creature Trait rules.

rows.name: Tail
textFields: The creatureâ€™s tail is capable of sweeping foes from their feet. They may lose Momentum to make a Free Attack that does SB +2 Damage. Smaller-Size targets that suffer any Wounds from the attack also gain the Prone Condition.

rows.name: Tentacles
textFields: The creature has a number of tentacles equal to #. They gain one Free Attack per tentacle. Each tentacleâ€™s attack does Damage of SB +0. If they cause Damage, they can also give their opponent an Entangled Condition, which will initiate a Grapple between the target and that tentacle. If a tentacle is Grappling, use the tentacleâ€™s Free Attack to resolve that Grapple, not the creatureâ€™s Action (see page 167).

rows.name: Territorial
textFields: This creature is protective of a particular area or location. They will fight to the death to protect it and will not normally pursue enemies if they flee this area.

rows.name: Terror
textFields: The creature supernaturally causes bone-chilling Terror. When first encountering the creature, opponents must make a Psychology Test (page 183). On a failure, opponents gain Broken Conditions equal to the Terror Rating, plus 1 for each negative SL. Regardless of the result, it also causes Fear (page 183) with an equal Fear Rating.

rows.name: Tongue
textFields: The creatureâ€™s prehensile tongue can wrap itself around prey, dragging it to a grisly end. They may lose Momentum to make a Free Attack. This is a Ranged Attack that does Damage of SB +0. It is up to the GM to decide on the range, though a default is 3 yards for creatures of Size (Small to Large) and 12 yards for larger creatures. If the attack hits, the target receives 1 Entangled Condition and, if a smaller Size, is dragged towards the creature, and is Engaged in melee combat. The creature can then choose whether to release the target, perform a Free Attack using its Weapon Trait, or keep the target wrapped in their tongue, initiating a Grapple (see page 167).

rows.name: Tracker
textFields: Trackers are adept at following their prey, generally through scent or hearing. The creature is granted the Track Skill at Int +10. This number may be increased at the GMâ€™s discretion.

rows.name: Trained
textFields: This Trait represents animals that have been trained through the Animal Training Skill. The skills the animal knows are marked in the parentheses. Feel free to create your own Trained skills. Broken: The animal is trained to ignore its Bestial Trait. It receives +2d10 Fellowship. Drive: The animal is trained to pull a coach, cart, plough, buggy, or similar. Entertain: The animal is trained to entertain others. It adds a +10 bonus to appropriate Entertain, Perform, or Play Tests. Fetch: The animal is trained to fetch. This is normally reserved for dogs and similar. Guard: The animal is trained to stay in one place or prowl around as a guard, granting it the Territorial Trait. Home: The animal is trained to return home if it is released or lost. Magic: The animal is trained to ignore Skittish when it comes to magic, which is required for most mounts used by spellcasters. Mount: The animal accepts a rider. Some creatures are especially belligerent, and will not accept a rider without the correct skill. For example, to ride a griffon, you need the Ride (Griffon) Skill. War: The animal is trained for war, gaining +10 Weapon Skill. It can also ignore Skittish for loud noises.

rows.name: Undead
textFields: The undead are neither living nor dead, meaning they are not reliant on the usual prerequisites for life such as air, food, water, and so on. This Trait most commonly comes into use when spells, Miracles, or other abilities affect Undead only.

rows.name: Unstable
textFields: The creatureâ€™s corpus is maintained by foul magics that are inherently unstable in the material realm. Whenever they end a Round Engaged with any opponents who possess Momentum when they do not, the creature is driven back, and the magics holding them together weaken and the creature loses 2 Wounds. If the creature ever reaches 0 Wounds, the magics holding them in place collapse, and they are destroyed or driven back from whence they came.

rows.name: Vampiric
textFields: The creature feeds on blood and draws great physical strength from this act. Whenever they perform a successful Bite attack against an appropriate opponent, they heal as many Wounds as the opponent loses. Drinking blood in this way is the only way they can heal.

rows.name: Venom
textFields: The creatureâ€™s attacks are poisoned or envenomed. When they cause Wounds, their opponent gains a Poisoned Condition. Some poisons are more potent than others, and the listed Difficulty should apply to Tests made to recover from the Poisoned Condition. See page 186.

rows.name: Vomit
textFields: Under duress, the creature can spew a stream of corrosive spew, dowsing their opponents in foul, semi-digested filth. If the creature starts their Turn engaged in combat, they can give up their Move and Action to activate their Vomit. The attacker performs an Opposed Ballistic Skill/Dodge Test against all targets within 2 yards (the attackerâ€™s single roll opposed by each individual target). The Test is Easy (+4 SL) for the vomiting creature, due to the close range, and Challenging (+0 SL) for opponents. All losing targets suffer a hit with TB +4 Damage and receive a Stunned condition. All weapons and armour carried by affected targets suffer 1 Damage as stomach acid corrodes them away. A creature may only Vomit once every 12 hours.

rows.name: Wallcrawler
textFields: The creature can effortlessly scale vertical surfaces and even traverse ceilings, ready to drop on unwary prey. They move at full Movement across any appropriate surface and automatically pass all Climb Tests.

rows.name: Ward
textFields: Perhaps because they are magical, wear a special talisman, or are just plain lucky, some blows just seem to miss. Roll 1d10 after any blow is received: if the roll is Rating or higher, the blow is ignored, even if it is a Critical.

rows.name: Web
textFields: The creature can create webbing to trap unwary foes. Whenever they successfully hit, opponents gain 1 Entangled Condition, with a Strength of the Rating given. See page 186.

rows.name: Ranged (Catapult)
textFields: Specialisations: Blackpowder, Bow, Crossbow, Engineering, Entangling, Explosives, Sling, Throwing. Anyone can throw a rock, but it takes training and practice to use weapons like bows, pistols, and throwing knives. Each Ranged Specialisation is specific to a group of ranged weapons. If you do not have the Ranged Specialisation for a weapon you wish to use, refer to Chapter 11: Consumer Guide for the penalties you will suffer when using the weapon.

rows.name: Crew Commander
textFields: Max: Initiative Bonus. Tests: Ranged Skill tests when firing a weapon with the Crewed Flaw. A Character with this talent is practised at managing crews of siege weapons and artillery pieces. The Character may make a Challenging (+0) Leadership Test to help a crew manning a weapon with the Crewed Quality within earshot. If the Character passes the Test, the crew members may then use the Character’s Ranged Skill when shooting the weapon.

rows.name: Etiquette (Mercenaries)
textFields: You can blend in socially with the chosen group, so long as you are dressed and acting appropriately. Furthermore, the GM may warn your Character if they begin to indulge in behaviour considered inappropriate by the social group. Example social groups include: Criminals, Cultists, Guilders, Nobles, and Soldiers.

rows.name: Craftsman (Fletcher)
textFields: You are a true creative talent, sufficiently skilled in a craft to have the potential to elevate it to an art form. Choose a Trade Specialisation. You gain Advantage on Tests of this skill, and may Advance it even if it is not part of your current Career. You may purchase this Talent more than once, choosing a new Trade Specialisation each time you do.

rows.name: Master Tradesman (Fletcher)
textFields: You are a skilled and reliable artisan. When you take this Talent, choose a Trade Specialisation. When you successfully use this Skill, you can choose to either use your rolled SL, or the number rolled on your units die. You may take this Talent more than once, choosing a new Trade Specialisation each time you do.

rows.name: Artistic (Cartography)
textFields: You have a natural talent for art. You may always advance the Art Skill, even if it is not part of your current Career. When you choose this Talent, pick one form of written or representative art, such as painting or poetry. You gain Advantage on Art Tests when working in that medium. You may purchase this Talent more than once, choosing another art form in which to excel.

rows.name: Savant (Artillery)
textFields: You are exceptionally learned and have a significant degree of specialised knowledge in your field of study. Choose any Lore Specialisation you possess. Tests made using this Lore Specialisation are made with Advantage. You may acquire this Talent more than once, choosing a new Lore Specialisation each time you do so.

rows.name: Fearless (Chaos)
textFields: You are either brave or crazy enough that fear of certain enemies has become a distant memory. When you take this Talent, choose any enemy group, such as Giants, Skeletons, or Trolls. You are immune to fear from enemies in the chosen group. You may acquire this Talent more than once, choosing a new enemy group each time you do so.

rows.name: Fearless (Cavalry)
textFields: You are either brave or crazy enough that fear of certain enemies has become a distant memory. When you take this Talent, choose any enemy group, such as Giants, Skeletons, or Trolls. You are immune to fear from enemies in the chosen group. You may acquire this Talent more than once, choosing a new enemy group each time you do so.

rows.name: Strong-Minded
textFields: You are the epitome of determination and resolve. Once per session, before taking a Test, you may choose to take that Test without any negative modifiers.

rows.name: Strike To Injure
textFields: You are an expert at striking your enemies’ most vulnerable areas. When rolling on a Critical Wound table, roll twice and choose which result you prefer. Further, you ignore the Called Shot penalty when going for a Silent Takedown (see page 135).

rows.name: Master Tradesman (Engineering)
textFields: You are a skilled and reliable artisan. When you take this Talent, choose a Trade Specialisation. When you successfully use this Skill, you can choose to either use your rolled SL, or the number rolled on your units die. You may take this Talent more than once, choosing a new Trade Specialisation each time you do.

rows.name: Command the Legion
textFields: Myrmidia carries your orders across the battlefield. You may issue a command to any ally within line of sight. The command must be relevant to the accomplishment of an armed struggle or ongoing strategy. Any Leadership Tests you make as a result benefit from a +10 bonus.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: Dismay Foe
textFields: You embody Myrmidia in her most wrathful of aspects. Gain the Terror 1 Creature Trait.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: In Good Order
textFields: Knowing that the situation is hopeless you pray that your forces do not suffer from a disastrous rout. While the miracle is in play any allies may break from combat without allowing the enemy to gain Momentum or make free attacks (the printed Fourth Edition cross-reference is Fleeing, WFRP p. 165).
rows.label: Magic

legacy.adaptation: Fourth Edition Advantage references converted to Momentum (core Appendix I).

rows.name: Know Your Enemy
textFields: You call on Myrmidia to inform you of a nearby enemy’s strengths and weaknesses. The GM should allow you to check the profile, traits, skills and talents of the target.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: On Deadly Ground
textFields: Knowing that victory cannot be secured unless your forces stand firm you call on Myrmidia to banish all thoughts of retreat from the minds of your allies. Whilst the miracle is in effect your allies do not receive Broken Conditions.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: Quick Strike
textFields: Infused with Myrmidia’s power, you benefit from heightened reflexes and can anticipate your opponent’s moves. At the start of every round whilst the Miracle is in effect, you may attempt a Challenging (+0) Initiative Test to gain an immediate free attack outside the normal turn sequence. This attack is resolved with whatever weapon you are carrying in your primary hand.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: Shieldmaiden’s Devotion
textFields: Your chanted prayers fill the hearts of the faithful with the fearlessness of her bravest Shieldmaidens. All Myrmidians within range gain +1 Fearless (Enemy) Talent. This enemy may either be a particular individual, or a particular species.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: Skill of Combat
textFields: You embody in your allies the skill of Myrmidia. Whilst this Miracle is in effect, all allies in range benefit from a +10 bonus to their WS and BS.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: Vengeful Wrath
textFields: You are filled with the righteous indignation of Myrmidia. Whilst this Miracle is in effect, you must charge and attack the nearest unrepentant enemy. You may reroll any Melee Skill rolls you make whilst the Miracle is in effect.
rows.label: Magic

rows.name: Youngblood
textFields: Max: 1. Tests: Any Social Tests with other Eonir. Your family are considered newcomers to the Laurelorn and are treated with condescension by Eonir of the older birth kindreds. You are always considered of lower Status than other Eonir, unless they also have the Youngblood Talent. Second generation Youngbloods can lose this Talent by passing a trial to join the Forestborn Kindred.

legacy.adaptation: Fourth Edition per-rank bonus on the listed Tests omitted; printed limit and effects retained under the approved Fifth Edition adaptation.

rows.name: Craftsman (Farmer)
textFields: You are a true creative talent, sufficiently skilled in a craft to have the potential to elevate it to an art form. Choose a Trade Specialisation. You gain Advantage on Tests of this skill, and may Advance it even if it is not part of your current Career. You may purchase this Talent more than once, choosing a new Trade Specialisation each time you do.

rows.name: Striding Gait (Woodlands)
textFields: You are experienced in traversing difficult ground. You ignore all movement penalties when crossing over or through a specified terrain. If engaged in a Pursuit in your chosen terrain, you receive +2 SL to all Tests relating to the Pursuit. Example Terrains are: Coastal, Desert, Rocky, Tundra, Wetland, Woodland. You may take this Talent more than once, choosing a new Terrain each time you do.
